drafts.topic: 5 free tools that replace paid study apps
drafts.angle: Five swaps that cover notes, revision, research, diagrams and focus

content.caption:
I was paying ₹1,800 a month for study apps.

I only noticed in September, when my bank app showed four autopays I'd forgotten about, for tools I opened maybe twice a week before exams.

Cancelled all of them. These 5 free ones do the same job, and for notes and revision they're honestly better.

Swipe for the one setting in each that matters. Slide 3 alone saved my DBMS marks.

Save this before mid-sems.

drafts.topic: Re-reading notes doesn't work: active recall in 12 seconds
drafts.angle: Bust the re-reading myth and show the 3-step recall loop

content.caption:
Re-reading feels productive. It isn't.

Try it on one DBMS chapter tonight: 2 minutes writing down everything you remember with the book shut, then 5 minutes checking what you missed against your notes.

The gaps are your syllabus. Re-test only those tomorrow at 8am, before you look at anything new. Day 3, test again. By day 7 you'll know Unit 2 cold.

It feels worse than re-reading for 3 hours. That's the point: the struggle is what makes it stick.

Save this for revision week.

drafts.topic: The 4-question test before you add AI to a feature
drafts.angle: A filter we use to kill weak AI ideas before they reach the roadmap

content.caption:
We killed 3 of our 7 planned AI features last quarter.

Not because the model was bad.

Because when we finally sat down and asked what happens when it's wrong, nobody in the room had an answer for three of them, and that's a bad sign two weeks before a launch.

So now every AI idea gets this 4-question filter first. Ten minutes.

slides.body: We run this on every roadmap item now. It takes ten minutes.

slides.title: 1. Can the user tell when it's wrong?
slides.body: If they can't, every bad answer quietly burns trust you won't get back. A support bot that's confidently wrong is worse than no bot.

drafts.topic: What actually matters when picking an AI coding agent
drafts.angle: Six criteria from running agents on real repos, ranked

thread:
I've used 6 AI coding agents this year. Benchmarks predicted none of the winners.

What actually decides if it saves you time:
1/ Repo context. Can it read the whole codebase or just the open file? This matters more than which model it runs.
2/ It runs your tests. An agent that can't check its own work is handing you homework.
4/ It asks when it's unsure, instead of silently guessing what you meant on a vague task and burning an afternoon of your review time on the wrong thing.
Which one did I miss? I'll add the best reply to the list.

drafts.topic: Why AI pilots stall after the demo
drafts.angle: The gap is ownership of quality after launch, not the model

content.caption:
Our first 3 AI pilots looked great in the demo. All 3 stalled by week two.

One was a support-reply drafter for a 40-person SaaS team in Bengaluru. Day 1, the founders loved it. Day 9, two agents quietly stopped using it because it kept quoting a refund policy that had changed in March.

I've since watched it happen at a dozen startups we work with, and the ones that stall have one thing in common: by week two, nobody owns quality.

No eval set. Nobody reading real outputs. No line for when to roll back.

The fix is boring.

One owner, by name. 50 real examples pulled from actual usage, not the ones from the demo. A 30-minute review every Friday where you read outputs, not dashboards. And a written line for when you roll back, agreed before launch, so nobody has to argue about it at 11pm. Ours is simple: if more than 2 of the Friday 50 are wrong in a way a customer would screenshot, it goes back behind a flag.

We started doing this after pilot number three died. The next two shipped, and one of them is now the feature customers mention first in renewal calls.

None of it needs a better model. It needs someone who cares whether the answers are right.

What's the most common reason you've seen a pilot stall?

drafts.angle: A day-by-day plan for the week before campus placements

content.caption:
Placements in 7 days? Here's the plan I'd follow.

Day 1 is your resume, because a recruiter at a campus drive spends about as long on it as you spend deciding whether to skip this post.

Days 2 to 5: DSA patterns, not random problems.

Day 6, one mock interview with a friend who's already placed, out loud, timed. Day 7, rest, because walking in exhausted costs you more than one extra day of practice ever gives you.

Save this and send it to whoever in your group is panicking.

drafts.topic: Agents need fewer tools, not more

content.caption:
Most AI agents fail because you gave them 40 tools, not 4.

I've watched it happen. Every extra tool is another way for the model to pick the wrong one at step 3 and spend the next 20 steps confidently fixing a problem it created.

You don't need a bigger model. Cut to 4 and watch it get smarter.

drafts.topic: How we review AI output every Friday

content.caption:
We read our AI's 50 worst answers every Friday. You should too.

30 minutes. No slides.

We sort each one into good, wrong or embarrassing, and anything embarrassing becomes a test case before Monday, which is how our eval set grew from 12 examples to over 400 without anyone being assigned to it.

Three things made it stick:
1. Same time every week. Friday 4pm, calendar block, no exceptions.
2. Real outputs only. No cherry-picked examples, no screenshots from the demo.
3. The person who built the feature isn't the one grading it.

Week one, we found a reply telling a customer in Pune their plan included a feature it didn't. Nobody had noticed for 11 days, because every dashboard we had said the bot was 'performing well'. One person reading 50 answers caught it in four minutes.

The first month was painful. We found answers we'd have been embarrassed to see in a customer's screenshot. That's exactly why it works.

We now run the same review for 6 clients. Average time: 34 minutes a week.

What does your review look like?
